Tag Questions with the Verb To Be
We use tag questions when we want to confirm what was said previously in a statement.

When we are almost sure about an idea, we can state it and then add a tag question in order to let the other person know that we expect him or her to confirm that statement.

Example: It is better to start with simple editors for learning HTML, isn't it?

The tag question verb depends on the verb we use in the statement. When the main verb of the sentence is the verb to be, we must also use the verb to be in the tag question.

Example: Professional HTML editors are much harder to use, aren't they?

Don't forget that if the statement is negative, the tag question should go in its affirmative form, and if it is affirmative the tag question should be negative.
As far as I'm concerned, websites are built by using some pre-determined basic tags, aren't they?
It is easier to create and modify web pages by using professional HTML editors, isn't it?
Reported Speech in Affirmative With the Verb Tell
The reported speech is used to inform what someone else says or said.

We need to take into account that in the reported speech, the verb tenses change depending on the verb that introduces the reported statement. Additionally, we generally use that to introduce the reported sentence; however, this is optional, especially in spoken English.

Example: My brother told me that he was learning how to design websites.

For the reported speech, we can use different verbs to introduce the reported statement, such as say, tell, or state. As of now, we are going to focus on the verb tell. All we need to know when using the verb tell, is that we need to inform to whom the person was talking to.

Example: The teacher told Sofia that she could start with simple editors before using the professional ones.

Moreover, we have to take into account that the verb tenses will depend on the tense of the verb we use to introduce the reported speech.

Examples:
The project manager tells us that it is necessary to learn how to write HTML.
The project manager told us that it was necessary to learn how to write HTML.

Notice that if the verb we use to introduce the reported speech is conjugated in the present tense, the verb in the reported speech will also be conjugated in a present tense (this happens when we talk about general statements or facts).

However, there is generally a shift tense when the reported speech is used:

Robert: Since we talked about HTML last time, I've been getting more interested in how it works and how it is used. As far as I'm concerned, websites are built by using some pre-determined basic tags, aren't they?

Albert: Exactly. Yesterday I spoke with one of my mentors and he explained to me the basic elements needed for the HTML documents. He told me that all documents must start with the document type declaration < ! DOCTYPE html >. Then, the text is organized and the appropriate tags are entered depending on how we want the webpage to look like.

My mentor also told me that the document itself begins with the opening tag < html > and ends with the closing tag < / html >, and that the body of the document is enclosed between the < body > and < / body > tags. After this, other tags are used like < h1 > for the first heading or < p > for paragraphs, along with their corresponding closing tags.

Robert: Wow! That sounds like a lot to bear in mind. However, I know that there are some special computer programs that are used for editing HTML and that some of them are more complex and allow people to work with related technologies such as Java. So, It is easier to create and modify web pages by using professional HTML editors, isn't it?

Albert: Not exactly. Most people have told me that it is better to start with simple text editors like Notepad or TextEdit. The best way to know you are on the right track is writing down the code, saving it and then trying it out by opening the saved file in a browser.

Robert: I'll put this into practice and I'm going to make use of my new tutorials. Thank you!
